Good evening. My name is Nancy Treanor, and I'm speaking on behalf of the Education Committee of the Fairfax County Federation of Citizens Associations. We'd like to begin our remarks by commending FCPS for communicating strong support for our teachers and other staff by focusing your advertised budget on compensation increases.

However, we are disappointed that a school system which emphasizes the data-driven classroom for its educators is seemingly not engaging in the same sort of rigorous data-driven analysis in developing its budget. FCPS requires frontline workers to check in with their students, see if what they're doing is working, and if not, to pivot and do something else.

We expect nothing less from FCPS in budget deliberations. We're aware, for example, that FCPS continues to face challenges in both attracting and retaining in-school personnel. However, FCPS has not proposed nor adopted significant changes to policies and/or regulations which aim to improve workforce satisfaction, nor has FCPS engaged in a root cause analysis regarding low teacher retention.

FCPS staffs its schools more generously than its peer divisions, but has not employed an efficiency analysis to determine whether those staffing standards are effective. We also continue to advocate that FCPS limit professional development and/or mandatory trainings to those with proven pedagogical impact in exchange for expanded teacher planning time.

We support the advertised budget's multi-year investments in programs with a strong history of providing benefit to students, such as athletics and fine and performing arts. We also applaud FCPS's continued investment in early childhood education. These investments are based on strong, data-driven thinking about what we know works best for kids.

As you engage in a more analytical and targeted approach to future budgets, FCPS may consider elevating the importance of the Office of Research and Strategic Improvement or ORSI. ORSI can help FCPS show your work in the same way that our students and teachers are held accountable through continual evaluation and proper oversight. Thank you for your time. Jennifer Ives, Emily Vanderhoff. Good evening Budget Chair Anderson, Dr. Reed and members of the board. My name is Emily

Vanderhoff. I'm a first grade teacher in FCPS and a proud member of FCFT. I first want to thank you you for introducing a strong needs-based budget that focused on competitive compensation. I know that you all are not at fault for the large shortfall we're facing. I'm disappointed in the decisions by the board of supervisors and state leaders that have left us here. I know the state budget deal was passed yesterday and I'm eager to see how the final amount may reduce some of the shortfall. As I'm sure you know, reducing the initially planned 6% MSA to 3% has been difficult for employees to hear. I know some on this board have asked to look at differentiating the pay increase to be more targeted. I read the response to Mr. McDaniel and Supervisor

Bierman's budget questions and realized there may be issues outside of my understanding to these suggestions, but I want to offer three considerations for differentiated increases. The staffing shortages are going to be felt differently across different positions. I would like to suggest taking into consideration the positions most hard hit by shortages for stronger increases to help with recruitment and retention. As a school system focused on serving students and knowing that student facing roles are some of the hardest to fill, I would suggest prioritizing those roles who directly impact students' school experience, including those who transport them to school, serve them a meal, keep the facility safe and comfortable, and provide instruction and services.

And finally, I know the responses in budget questions mentioned a delicate balance in the spacing between pay scales, but this board has also acknowledged in the past that support staff pay is not sufficient. For example, the three-year plan to raise the CIS scale to 50% of the teacher scale was noted at the time as just the start for improving pay for support staff.

While 3% across the board seems fair on the surface it results in a vastly different dollar amount from employee to employee, advantaging those with higher salaries. I would suggest finding a way to raise the percentage of the lowest paid workers to begin to close the gap and provide a more equitable distribution of the amount that we have.
Thank you for the time to share my thoughts. I know that the decisions before you are not easy and I appreciate the thought and care you are giving to the process. Thank you.

Our mission for public education is to champion public schools as the cornerstone of a healthy democracy and the right for every child to an exceptional education, which is why we support fully funded schools and associated equity initiatives that ensure each student receives the support and resources that they need to succeed.

Thus, we ask that greater funding be directed to those who are most vulnerable and underserved like Title I schools, lower-income students, English language learners, and students requiring special education services. The families of the most vulnerable students, as you know, often have the quietest voices, so please listen closely and respond to their needs.

Another equity issue is that recent literacy initiatives in elementary may be leaving a lot of secondary school students behind. We have so many smart, capable high schoolers whose poor literacy skills may make college inaccessible. Please don't shut them out from a lifetime of opportunities.

Finally, the proposed 3% pay raise still leaves Fairfax teachers behind. Being underpaid combined with the actions of a few bad actors, some of which are parents, operatives, and even some who are administrators, will have short and long-term consequences in attracting and retaining amazing teachers.

I've heard many complaining about taxes, especially on Nextdoor, and how much money is allocated for our school students and educators. Those complaints really fail to recognize the long-term consequences of an undereducated Fairfax County population, which means fewer and or less qualified doctors, nurses, medical technicians and health aides, all of which we need with a rapidly aging population in Fairfax County.

I've met Fairfax graduates in the ER at enumerable times because we're an accident-prone family. And they are the best they can be because they came from this school system. And I'd hate for that to change. Thank you.
